```{r setup-linearity, include=FALSE}
library(here)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, dpi = 110)
source(here("analysis", "reports", "descriptive_plots", "R", "trend_analysis.R"))
```

```{=html}
<h1 id="linearity-use-policy">Linearity: middelengebruik en beleidsvoorkeur</h1>

<div class="block-box">
<strong>What is paired with what.</strong> The main study asks own use for four
substance <em>groups</em> &mdash; alcohol, tabak, softdrugs and harddrugs &mdash;
so each policy slider is paired with the use item of its group: alcohol with
alcohol, nicotine with tabak, cannabis with softdrugs, and psychedelica, MDMA,
cocaine, speed and heroine each with harddrugs. Painkillers belong to no group
and are left out. The use item is ordered: nooit &rarr; niet in het laatste jaar
&rarr; wel eens &rarr; vaak.
<br><br>
<strong>Trend analysis.</strong> A one-way ANOVA over an ordered predictor has
<em>k</em>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 degrees of freedom between groups. Trend analysis
splits them into a <strong>linear</strong> component (1&nbsp;df: the regression
of the slider on the level index 1,&nbsp;2,&nbsp;3,&nbsp;4) and a
<strong>deviation-from-linearity</strong> remainder
(<em>k</em>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;2&nbsp;df). Both are tested against the
within-groups mean square the omnibus <em>F</em> uses.
<br><br>
A significant linear term means the slider moves monotonically across the use
levels. A non-significant deviation term means the group means sit close enough
to a line for the variable to enter a later model as one numeric term rather
than <em>k</em>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 dummies.
<br><br>
<strong>Slider direction.</strong> 0&nbsp;=&nbsp;<em>verbod</em>,
100&nbsp;=&nbsp;<em>vrije verkoop</em>, so a positive slope means heavier users
prefer more permissive policy.
</div>
```

```{r trend-diagonal, echo=TRUE}
# The pairing is USE_OF_SUBSTANCE (data.R): substance -> the use
# item of its group. POLICY_COLUMNS is keyed by the same substance names.
trend_substances <- names(USE_OF_SUBSTANCE)

trend_diagonal <- do.call(rbind, lapply(trend_substances, function(s)
  trend_test(pilot[[POLICY_COLUMNS[[s]]]], pilot[[USE_OF_SUBSTANCE[[s]]]])))

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    middel           = trend_substances,
    n                = trend_diagonal$n,
    k                = trend_diagonal$k,
    `F linear`       = round(trend_diagonal$F_lin, 2),
    `p linear`       = round(trend_diagonal$p_lin, 3),
    `F deviation`    = round(trend_diagonal$F_dev, 2),
    `p deviation`    = round(trend_diagonal$p_dev, 3),
    `eta squared`    = round(trend_diagonal$eta2, 3),
    `linear share`   = paste0(round(100 * trend_diagonal$lin_share), "%"),
    `slope per step` = round(trend_diagonal$slope, 1),
    check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = paste("Own use against own policy slider. 'Linear share' is the",
                  "proportion of all group differences that a straight line",
                  "already accounts for; 'slope per step' is the slider",
                  "movement, in points, per level of use."))
```

*k* is the number of populated use levels; the five harddrugs rows share one
use item, so they share its levels.

```{r trend-contrasts, echo=TRUE}
# Why a second table: the four levels are not four steps of one thing. The
# nooit -> vroeger step is "have you ever tried it"; vroeger -> soms -> vaak is
# "how often". The contrasts in trend_contrasts() ask those two separately.
# (trend_frame() factors the column, so the levels are the four answer options
# whatever they are numbered - the 0-based use levels give the same test.)
trend_split <- do.call(rbind, lapply(trend_substances, function(s)
  trend_contrasts(pilot[[POLICY_COLUMNS[[s]]]],
                  pilot[[USE_OF_SUBSTANCE[[s]]]], label = s)))

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    middel                = trend_split$label,
    n                     = trend_split$n,
    `F ever tried`        = round(trend_split$F_ever,  2),
    `p ever tried`        = round(trend_split$p_ever,  3),
    `F frequency`         = round(trend_split$F_users, 2),
    `p frequency`         = round(trend_split$p_users, 3),
    `F curvature`         = round(trend_split$F_curv,  2),
    `p curvature`         = round(trend_split$p_curv,  3),
    check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = paste("The same 3 df, split into three orthogonal contrasts:",
                  "ever tried vs never (-3, 1, 1, 1), the frequency gradient",
                  "among those who have (0, -1, 0, 1), and curvature among",
                  "them (0, 1, -2, 1). Heroine is blank because it has only",
                  "three populated levels."))
```

The `ever tried` contrast separates level 1 from levels 2-4; the frequency
contrast compares levels 2 and 4 among those who have used the substance.

```{r trend-diagonal-plot, echo=TRUE, fig.height=8.5, fig.width=9.5}
# One panel per substance so linearity can be judged by eye: the observed cell
# means (blue) against the straight line fitted through them (dashed grey).
# The gap between the two IS the deviation-from-linearity term.
USE_LEVEL_LABELS <- c("nooit", "niet in\nlaatste jaar", "wel eens", "vaak")

# One row per respondent per substance. This is the only data frame the figure
# needs: the cell means, their intervals and the fitted line are all summaries
# of it, so ggplot computes them rather than the chunk precomputing them.
trend_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(trend_substances, function(s) {
  d <- pilot[c(POLICY_COLUMNS[[s]], USE_OF_SUBSTANCE[[s]])]
  names(d) <- c("beleid", "gebruik")
  cbind(middel = s, d[complete.cases(d), ])
}))
trend_long$middel <- factor(trend_long$middel, levels = trend_substances)

# A cell of one respondent has no standard error. Rather than let mean_se
# return NA and drop the row with a warning, its interval collapses to the
# point itself - nothing is hidden, and the printed n says how thin it is.
mean_ci <- function(v) {
  if (length(v) < 2) return(data.frame(y = mean(v), ymin = mean(v),
                                       ymax = mean(v)))
  mean_se(v, mult = 1.96)
}

ggplot(trend_long, aes(x = gebruik, y = beleid)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.17, height = 0, colour = "grey70", alpha = 0.35,
              size = 0.7) +
  # the straight line the deviation term is measured against
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed",
              colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.5) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", colour = "#3B6EA5",
               linewidth = 0.8) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_ci, colour = "#3B6EA5", size = 0.4) +
  # cell n's sit in a strip below the slider range, clear of the responses
  stat_summary(fun.data = function(v)
                 data.frame(y = -6, label = paste0("n=", length(v))),
               geom = "text", size = 2.3, colour = "grey45") +
  facet_wrap(~ middel, ncol = 3) +
  # the x axis IS the use level, so the breaks are the levels themselves
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = USE_NEVER:USE_OFTEN, labels = USE_LEVEL_LABELS,
                     expand = expansion(add = 0.35)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-11, 100), breaks = seq(0, 100, 25)) +
  labs(x = "Hoe vaak heb je het gebruikt?",
       y = "Beleidsvoorkeur (0 = verbod, 100 = vrije verkoop)",
       title = "Policy preference by own use, per substance",
       subtitle = paste0(
         "Blue: observed cell means with 95% CI. ",
         "Dashed grey: the straight line fitted through them.\n",
         "The gap between the two is what the deviation-from-linearity test ",
         "measures. Cell n's are printed under each point.")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = 9),
        strip.text    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9),
        axis.text.x   = element_text(size = 7, colour = "grey25"),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

```{=html}
<div class="block-box">
<strong>How much weight these results can carry.</strong> Three cautions, all
of them about the size of the soft launch rather than about the method.
<br><br>
<strong>The deviation test is a non-rejection.</strong> Passing it means there
is no reason to object to treating the variable as ordinal &mdash; not that
linearity has been demonstrated. With this <em>n</em> the test has limited power
to detect a bend, so a clean deviation row is permission, not proof.
<br><br>
<strong>The linear p-values are uncorrected.</strong> Nine tests run here, and
many more elsewhere in this tab. Treat any single <em>p</em> just under .05 as a
lead to confirm in the main study.
<br><br>
<strong>Some cells are nearly empty.</strong> The upper use levels of softdrugs
and harddrugs hold only a few respondents; the plot prints every cell
<em>n</em> for exactly this reason. Where a flag rests on such a cell it is a
cell-size artefact, and the main-study sample is what will settle it.
</div>
```
